  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent services
  to enhance the quality of life for our entire community.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos.Per the Americans with Disabilities
Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359
for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with another
person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City Council
may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted up to 24
hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov.

While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City Council to take action on any
item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.

4.  PUBLIC HEARING:

4-A.  CONSIDERATION AND POSSIBLE ACTION TO ADOPT ORDINANCES
  ESTABLISHING WATER AND WASTEWATER (SEWER) RATES

  On July 16, 2014, the City Council adopted Ordinance Nos. 2109 and 2110
  adjusting the rates for water and sewer, respectively. These Ordinances included
  a 10% to 15% increase in rates for a five-year period beginning September 2014.
  The Ordinances also included an automatic reversal of utility rate charges effective
  August 2019 back to utility charges existing in August of 2017. Since that time,
  several factors have changed: declines in water usage resulting from increased
  efficiency and an increase in operating costs due to inflation. A new
  comprehensive rate study was desirable.

  Page 14 of 134

On June 16, 2021, the Council authorized the City Manager to execute an
agreement with HF&H Consultants, LLC (HF&H) for a Utility Rate Fees Study (the
Study). The last comprehensive study on the water, wastewater, and refuse rates
occurred in 2014.

HF&H has worked with City staff to develop comprehensive rate analyses for the
water and wastewater (sewer) enterprises with recommendations that ensure the
rates charged are fair and equitable to the City's users and can adequately fund
the City’s operations of these services.
Public Speakers:

-  Rick Simonson, Vice-President, HF & H Consultants, LLC., virtually present,
  contributed to a PowerPoint presentation and discussed how the sewer and
  water rates proposals were determined and how those new sewer and water
  rates in different examples would affect residents.

-  Carlos Garcia voiced his opposition to the rate increases saying that the City is
  not reporting expenditures originating from the sewer fees and stated he
  believes the City receives a return on the investment of fees received that
  should be enough to allocate for the repairs required.

-  Andy Islas voiced his opposition to the rate increases citing his confusion over
  the information that is being presented to residents in the protest ballot packet
  and appealed to the City Council to consider residents with fixed incomes and
  suggested including this issue in a regularly scheduled election.

-  Armen Sebastian appealed to the City Council to consider the impact of the
  rate increases on senior citizens and those with fixed incomes and cited the
  2022 sales tax measure whose funds were supposed to protect local drinking
  water and suggested the City utilize those funds toward infrastructure repairs.

-  Teresa Real Sebastian expressed her opposition to the proposed rate
  increases and cited her opinion on the difference in the rates proposed in the
  PowerPoint presentations versus the rates proposed in the Proposition 218
  notices that were sent to residents. She mentioned an alleged error on the
  protest ballot portion of the Spanish-translated Proposition 218 notice that she
  stated caused confusion for Spanish-speaking residents. She submitted copies
  of the Spanish translated sewer and water rate Proposition 218 notices where
  the alleged error is to the City Clerk which were received and filed. She stated
  that there has been a lack of transparency in the process by pointing out that
  justification for the new rates is not taking into account state-mandated water
  conservation in 2017 which lowered City revenue.

-  Wing Law expressed his confusion regarding the Proposition 218 notice and
  protest ballot, stating that the ballot had insufficient space for residents to fill in
  their parcel and account information, the print size being too small, and the
  water and sewer notices being so identical to each other as to cause confusion
  for residents. He also asked for more transparency regarding expenditures
  related to the fees received by the City. He continued to state that residents
  were not informed what the threshold was for protest ballots to alter the
  outcome, and that many residents he spoke to were unaware that the City was
  undertaking a Proposition 218 process.

-  Maychelle Yee, a resident expressed her concern when she was told there was
  no sewer plan, yet the City is asking residents to pay more for services with no
  plan as to expenditures. She asked for transparency in the process, and more
  effort on the part of staff to inform the City Council and the public.

-  Carmen Reyes gave her time to Randolph Reyes.

-  Randolph Reyes voiced his opposition to the proposed rate increases, stating
  the increases are unusually high as they add to the taxes that are already on
  the water bill, and stated that the calculations are using inaccurate billing
  periods since residents are billed bi-monthly and the rate calculations are
  presented as monthly amounts. He stated that the rate increases are unfair to
  low and fixed income residents.

Discussion: Finance Director Garcia presented a PowerPoint presentation
detailing background and infrastructure, which included the public notice, protest
ballot process, infrastructure needs such as water meter replacement, emergency
replacement of water and sewer facilities, past expenditures, rate-making
objectives and considerations, the rate study process, and historical water
revenue and expenses. Finance Director Garcia reviewed options for utility billing
assistance available to the public including contacting water billing to discuss
alternative payment arrangements, the Lifeline Discount Program, and the State
of California Department of Community Services and Development Low Income
Household Water Assistance Program and mentioned the Chinatown Service
Center Utility Assistance Program. Public Works Director Igoe talked about the
planning and prioritizing process for the Capital Improvement Projects and the
examples of infrastructure failure on display in the Council Chamber. The City
Council and City Attorney also touched on the safe water protocols which were
mentioned and the limited scope of use for funding earmarked for safe water
programs. Finance Director Garcia provided information regarding the translated
material in the Proposition 218 notice. City Manager Alvarez added that staff are
actively looking at grant opportunities, zero percent interest loans, and other
opportunities that the City can offer to assist utility customers.

the public hearing; (2) receiving all written and verbal testimony regarding the

initiative measure to the November 5, 2024 ballot. If approved by voters, the initiative
measure would add Chapter 5.92 (HEALTHCARE WORKERS MINIMUM WAGE) to Title

BACKGROUND
The City of Monterey Park received a FEMA grant in the amount of $82,101.88 with a
City match of $8,210.90 totaling $90,312.07 for the replacement of the exhaust system
and ancillaries at Fire Station 61.

The current system is over 20 years old and has reached its useful service life. The
vehicle exhaust system (“System”) consists of four hoses strategically placed throughout
the various bays. The purpose of the System is to capture emissions expelled by the
vehicles as they enter the facility. Currently, firefighters are only able to connect the
System to the apparatuses after they are partially or completely in the station. Therefore,
emissions are not completely removed, but instead, some are released into the facility,
which may expose staff to exhaust emissions from these vehicles. Staff seeks to update
the System, by replacing current equipment with longer hoses and tracks to allow
firefighters to connect the hoses to the apparatuses prior to entering the station. The
System will be able capture more exhaust and diminish exposure of exhaust emissions.

The City would ordinarily need to comply with the competitive bidding requirements of the
California Public Contracts code for this project. Here, however, competitive bidding
would not affect the final result. Specifically, each vehicle exhaust removal system is
unique in its own way and has not been standardized to the degree that they are
commodities which can be subjected to competitive bid. Each exhaust system is covered
by a patent and specifications particularly and exactly describing one system would
necessarily exclude others.

FISCAL IMPACT
The City of Monterey Park is using the grant funding to enter into an agreement with Air
Exchange to provide labor and material for the replacement of the exhaust system and
ancillaries under the terms of the grant. This project is funded by the FEMA grant in the
amount of $82,101.88 with a City match of $8,210.90 for a total of $90,312.07.

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. As early as the 17th century, Africans were forcibly brought to American shores to
  be enslaved, and Black Americans have subsequently faced systemic injustices of
  lynch mobs, segregation, racist attacks, discrimination, and denial of basic,
  fundamental rights.

  B. Black Americans, despite said injustices that continue to exist today, have made
  significant contributions to the economic, educational, political, artistic, literary,
  scientific, and technological advancements of the United States.

  C. In 1915, Dr. Carter G. Woodson founded the Association for the Study of Negro
  Life and History (presently known as the Association for the Study of African
  American Life and History), and in 1926, established “Negro History Week” to
  honor the history of African Americans and their contributions to American Life.

  D. In 1976, the Association for the Study of African American Life and History
  influenced the week-long observance to a month in honor of the Nation’s
  bicentennial. It has remained a month-long commemoration ever since.

  E. National Black History Month in February celebrates the legacy of Black and
  African Americans whose power to lead, overcome, and expand the meaning and
  practice of American democracy has helped the Nation become a more fair and
  just society.

  F. Since the mid-1970s, every United States President, regardless of political party,
  has issued messages and proclamations recognizing the significance of National
  Black History Month by urging all Americans to recognize the important
  contributions made by Black Americans to American life and culture.

  G. The United States Congress has also passed laws and adopted resolutions
  recognizing the significance and contributions made by Black Americans since
  1986.

  H. The Library of Congress, National Archives and Records Administration, National
  Endowment for the Humanities, National Gallery of Art, National Park Service,
  Smithsonian Institution, and the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum pay
  tribute to the generations of African Americans who struggled with adversity to
  achieve full citizenship in American society.
